analysis.one_liner: Gives uninsured people free insulin and taxes drug makers who spike insulin prices.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Finance Committee, received no vote in either chamber, and died with zero cosponsors when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would create a program giving uninsured and underinsured people with a prescription free insulin through state-issued cards — a 7-day emergency supply within 5 business days, then a 90-day supply. To pay for it, insulin manufacturers would pay annual fees based on their market share, and any manufacturer that raised an insulin price faster than inflation would owe an excise tax of 50% to 100% of the extra revenue. The bill would also cut the monopoly period for copycat versions of biological drugs from 12 years to 7 years, bringing cheaper biosimilar competition sooner.
analysis.who_benefits: People with diabetes who have no insurance or are in high-deductible plans, tribal communities, and patients who would eventually get cheaper biosimilar insulin once the exclusivity period shortens.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Uninsured and underinsured people with diabetes

how_it_helps.text: States, Indian tribes, and tribal organizations would get federal grants to issue insulin cards: an initial card valid for about a 7-day supply within 5 business days of applying, and a card for an approximate 90-day supply within 12 business days, filled at participating pharmacies at no cost to the individual [S3].
Payments the program makes for an underinsured person's insulin would count toward that person's health plan deductible or other out-of-pocket costs [S2].
The program would be funded by annual fees on insulin manufacturers, each paying a share proportional to its insulin sales, with total fees equal to the program's cost [S2].

Manufacturers that raise an insulin price above the inflation rate would owe an excise tax on the extra revenue: 50% of the price-spike revenue for smaller spikes, 75% for spikes of 15-20%, and 100% for spikes of 20% or more, with the tax also applying cumulatively to multi-year run-ups [S3].
Cutting the marketing exclusivity period for biological drugs from 12 to 7 years would let lower-priced biosimilar versions reach the market five years earlier [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Insulin manufacturers, who would fund the program through market-share fees and pay excise taxes of up to 100% of revenue from inflation-beating price increases; brand biologic makers would also lose five years of market exclusivity.

drawbacks.text: The grant program would sunset after five years, so the free-insulin cards would be temporary rather than a lasting fix [S3].
States would have to contribute $1 of their own money for every $3 in federal funds, so states unwilling or unable to pay their share would leave their residents uncovered [S3].

The bill taxes price spikes rather than capping insulin prices, so base prices above inflation's reach would remain untouched, and manufacturers could argue higher prices were justified by input costs to seek an exemption [S3].

The pharmaceutical industry's standard objection — that a shorter exclusivity period reduces the incentive to invest in developing new biological medicines — would apply to the 12-to-7-year change, a cost honest supporters would have to weigh.
The program requires an application process with proof of residency and prescriptions, which creates paperwork and waiting periods that some people in immediate need might not navigate [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people rationing insulin because they cannot afford it, the card program would deliver immediate, tangible relief at no cost to them, and the manufacturer fees mean the program pays for itself rather than adding to the deficit. The design is narrower than a price cap: it targets the uninsured and underinsured rather than everyone, lasts only five years, and leaves manufacturers free to charge any base price as long as they do not spike it above inflation. The exclusivity cut is the strongest cost-containment tool, but its benefits arrive years after enactment. On balance the bill's benefits to patients outweigh its costs, which fall mainly on the manufacturers whose pricing prompted it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Tina Smith introduced the bill in the Senate on May 9, 2023 [S5].
The same day it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Finance, where no further action was ever taken [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor during the entire Congress [S4].
The bill died when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, without ever coming to a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Insulin manufacturers are better off: they avoided the market-share fees, the excise tax on price spikes, and a five-year cut to biologic exclusivity, while uninsured patients continued to face the prices the bill targeted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insulin manufacturers, and no one else

for.name: Sen. Tina Smith
for.role: U.S. Senator from Minnesota, sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Emergency Access to Insulin Act of 2023 and referred it to the Finance Committee.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Ron Wyden (D-OR)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no vote — in the 20 months before the Congress ended.

against.name: Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: None joined as cosponsors during the entire two-year Congress, despite a member of their own caucus sponsoring the bill.

against.name: Insulin manufacturers
against.role: The three companies that control roughly 90% of the U.S. insulin market
against.what_they_did: The pharmaceutical industry has consistently opposed legislation that taxes drug price increases and shortens market exclusivity periods.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows no votes on the bill at all: one Democrat sponsored it, no member of either party cosponsored it, and it died in committee without a hearing or roll call.

industries.industry: Insulin manufacturers (Eli Lilly, Novo Nordisk, Sanofi)
industries.note: The bill would charge each manufacturer an annual fee proportional to its insulin sales to fund free-insulin programs, and impose an excise tax of 50% to 100% of any revenue gained from price increases above inflation. Ordinary people who ration insulin because of cost would gain directly from the same provisions that cost these companies revenue.

Cutting the marketing exclusivity period for biological drugs from 12 to 7 years would end these companies' monopoly five years earlier, letting cheaper biosimilars compete sooner. Patients would eventually see lower prices as a result.

The program would require states to sign agreements with pharmacies to fill insulin prescriptions for cardholders and pay the pharmacies for that insulin, bringing in guaranteed reimbursement for dispensing insulin to people who currently may not fill those prescriptions at all.

Plans would have to count program-paid insulin costs toward enrollees' deductibles, moving underinsured patients toward coverage faster at no direct cost to the insurer, since the state program pays the pharmacy.
